content: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a medical condition that can occur in women who use certain fertility medications designed to stimulate egg production. It is a potential complication of fertility treatments. The symptoms of OHSS can vary in severity. Most women experience mild symptoms, which may include abdominal bloating, mild abdominal pain, and weight gain. However, in rare cases, more severe symptoms can develop. These include significant weight gain (more than 10 pounds within 3 to 5 days), severe abdominal pain or swelling, reduced urination, and shortness of breath. OHSS occurs when fertility medications overstimulate the ovaries, causing them to become enlarged and leading to fluid leakage into the abdominal and chest cavities. This condition typically arises after ovulation, particularly when a hormone called human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is administered to trigger ovulation. The risk of OHSS increases if multiple doses of hCG are given or if pregnancy occurs during the same cycle. Women under 35 years of age, those with very high estrogen levels during fertility treatments, or those with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) are at higher risk. OHSS is more commonly associated with injectable fertility medications and is rare in women who only take oral fertility drugs. Up to 10% of women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) may develop OHSS, though most cases are mild. It is important to seek urgent medical care if you experience symptoms such as rapid weight gain (more than 5 pounds in a single day), severe abdominal pain, persistent nausea that prevents you from eating or drinking, reduced urination, shortness of breath, or dizziness. In cases of severe OHSS, a healthcare provider will closely monitor your condition. You may need to be hospitalized. Mild cases of OHSS typically do not require medical treatment. To alleviate symptoms, you should rest with your legs elevated, drink plenty of fluids (especially those containing electrolytes), and avoid alcohol, caffeine, intense exercise, and sexual activity. Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen (Tylenol) can help manage discomfort. It is also important to monitor your weight daily to detect any rapid increases. Severe cases of OHSS may require hospitalization, where intravenous fluids will be administered, excess fluid will be drained, and your condition will be closely observed. Most mild cases of OHSS resolve on their own after menstruation begins. Severe cases may take several days to improve, and symptoms can persist for weeks if pregnancy occurs during OHSS. Rarely, OHSS can lead to life-threatening complications, such as blood clots, kidney failure, severe electrolyte imbalances, or significant fluid accumulation in the abdomen or chest. To prevent OHSS, your doctor will carefully monitor your response to fertility medications using blood tests and pelvic ultrasounds. If your estrogen levels rise too quickly or too high, your doctor may adjust your medication dosage or temporarily halt treatment. In some cases, a protein solution called albumin may be administered to reduce the risk of OHSS.
